newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares close mixed in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares close mixed in quiet trade.

text.p: Undervalued shares on the illiquid second tier of the Russian Trading System were some of the more active areas of the market, along with shares in Norilsk Nickel, in an overall unexciting market on Friday, traders said.
But they saw the possibility for leading shares to hot up on the back of results, expected next week, from the sale of a 38 percent stake in Norilsk.
The RTS 22-share index rose to 510.20 from 506.45 on Thursday. Total market volume was a lacklustre $44.4 million.

"There was a lot of play surrounding Nickel after the news of the share conversions," said ING Barings trader Oleg Galkin, referring to the company's morning announcement that preferred shares would be convertible into ordinaries after the sale.
"People are not sure about this conversion and whether it will happen or not. Some are trying to sell and others are trying to buy."
Official closing prices were unavailable, but preferred Norilsk shares last traded at $13.5 after $12.90 previously and ordinaries at $15.00 after $15.30.
"The conversion would be bad for ordinary shares -- it would be like a hidden dilution," Galkin said.
Among leading shares, national power company UES firmed to $0.4240 from $0.4190 and Yuganskneftegaz, which registered the biggest turnover for a single stock, rose to $34.75 from $34.10.
International long-distance carrier Rostelekom dipped to $4.85 from $4.90.
Dealers said second tier stocks, particularly regional tyre companies and tube works, were picking up on Western interest.

"It was mostly Russian money buying blue chips -- Western investors were buying on the second tier," said Prospekt's head of overseas trading Igor Lossavio. "People are willing to invest money and are looking at new companies."
But Galkin said news from the sale of the Norilsk stake could spark activity on the broader market next week.
"We can expect some move in Norilsk after this and maybe it will push the market somewhere, depending on the news," he said.
